hints: Start by recalling what floods into the sarcoplasm from the sarcoplasmic reticulum just before contraction begins, and which thin-filament protein detects it.
Think about what covers the myosin-binding sites on actin at rest, and how a shape change in its neighbour protein moves it out of the way.
Once the sites on actin are exposed, consider what the thick filament protein does to link the two types of filament together.
For the final mark, link the pulling action to the visible shortening of the sarcomere and remember why ATP is needed to repeat the cycle.
walkthrough:
Calcium as the Trigger - Troponin Acts as Sensor**
When an action potential arrives, $Ca^{2+}$ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the sarcoplasm. Troponin, found on the thin filament, binds this $Ca^{2+}$ and changes its 3D shape. This is the switch that starts everything.

Unblocking Actin - Tropomyosin Moves**
At rest tropomyosin lies across actin and physically blocks the myosin-binding sites. When troponin changes shape it pulls tropomyosin away, so the binding sites on actin are now exposed and available.

Cross-Bridges and Power Stroke - Myosin Does the Work**
Exposed actin allows myosin heads from the thick filament to bind and form cross-bridges. The myosin head then bends and performs the power stroke, pulling the actin filament past myosin toward the centre. This slides the filaments and shortens the sarcomere, so Z lines move closer together toward the M line.

ATP for Detachment - Resetting the Cycle**
Myosin heads have ATPase activity. Binding of a new ATP molecule lets the myosin head detach from actin, ready to re-attach further along if $Ca^{2+}$ is still present. Without ATP the bridge cannot release.

Final answer: Troponin binds $Ca^{2+}$ and changes shape; tropomyosin moves away exposing myosin-binding sites on actin; myosin heads bind actin to form cross-bridges; myosin performs power stroke pulling actin so sarcomere shortens / Z lines move closer; binding of ATP to myosin allows detachment for next cycle. Any four points.

hints: Recall what acetylcholine normally does at the muscle membrane after release into the synaptic cleft, and what a similar-shaped molecule could do there.
Think about the type of channel protein linked to the acetylcholine receptor and which ion normally rushes in through it.
Connect failure of that ion movement to the electrical change needed in the sarcolemma to trigger $Ca^{2+}$ release and contraction.
walkthrough:
Normal Signalling at the Neuromuscular Junction**
Normally acetylcholine released from the motor neurone binds to specific receptors on the muscle sarcolemma. Those receptors are linked to chemically-gated $Na^{+}$ channels. Binding opens the channels, $Na^{+}$ floods in, and the membrane depolarises to start a muscle action potential.

Blocking by a Mimic**
Succinylcholine has a similar shape to acetylcholine, so it fits into and blocks the acetylcholine receptors. It acts as a competitive inhibitor but does not trigger the normal opening response. Because the true transmitter cannot bind, the $Na^{+}$ channels stay closed.

No Sodium Entry Means No Contraction**
With channels closed, $Na^{+}$ cannot enter the muscle cell sarcoplasm. The sarcolemma therefore stays polarised and no action potential spreads along the T-tubules. Without depolarisation there is no $Ca^{2+}$ release and the sliding filament mechanism in (a) cannot start, so the muscle stays paralysed.

Final answer: Succinylcholine binds to acetylcholine receptors as a competitive inhibitor; $Na^{+}$ channel proteins do not open; $Na^{+}$ do not enter sarcoplasm; sarcolemma / postsynaptic membrane is not depolarised so no action potential and no contraction.

hints: Use the clue that mainly boys are affected to think about which sex chromosome could carry the dystrophin gene.
Consider whether the disease allele must be dominant or recessive, given that the disease is rare at 4 in 100000.
Compare how many copies of that chromosome boys (XY) and girls (XX) have, and what that means for showing a recessive trait.
walkthrough:
Location - A Gene on the X Chromosome**
The pattern of mainly boys affected points to sex linkage. The dystrophin gene is on the X chromosome. Boys inherit their single X from their mother, girls inherit two Xs, one from each parent.

Recessive Behaviour - Why It Is Rare**
The DMD allele is recessive. That means its effect is masked by a normal dominant allele. This fits the low frequency, because most copies of the allele are hidden in healthy carriers.

Why Boys Show It More Often**
A boy is XY and hemizygous - he has only one copy of every X-linked gene. If that one X carries the DMD allele he has no normal allele to mask it, so he develops the disease. A girl would need the recessive allele on both Xs to develop DMD. A girl with one normal and one DMD allele is a heterozygous carrier with normal dystrophin and no symptoms.

Final answer: DMD gene is sex-linked on the X chromosome and recessive; males are XY with only one X chromosome / one allele so one recessive allele causes DMD; females are XX so heterozygotes are unaffected carriers, only homozygous recessive females develop DMD.
